items.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: Lester Young could compose in eight bars, something that you can study the rest of your life.

ctx.x: Well I think it’s a lot more fun to do than it is to listen to. I think that’s one of the problems with the music, with a lot of that. It can become very self-indulgent. And when I started playing with Ruby and George, everything was thought of as — solos weren’t too long — they used Benny’s trios and quartets as a good example of where nobody played too long, there were no 40 chorus solos, and musicians were standing around talking to one another. It was thought out with the audience in mind, but also from, I…

melody and shape — as much as whether the audience is going to like it or not. And I got wrapped up in that too, and it’s to the point now where I can’t stand — as a bass player sometimes I find myself in those situations where the horn players are playing chorus after chorus after chorus, and I’m getting bored, so I can imagine how the audience is feeling. Because I’ve got something to do. And I really think the discipline of that kind of thing is really important in a player, is to — Lester Young could compose…
If you were talking to a group of young musicians, which I know you do a lot, can you describe how you think of your role as a bassist?
